chief_complaint: aching shoulder pain when reaching overhead
hpi_details: 20F with gradual aching shoulder pain provoked by overhead reaching; clarify duration, activity changes, trauma, and objective weakness on focused assessment.
ideas: She thinks she strained a shoulder muscle from carrying a heavy backpack across campus or sleeping awkwardly on it.
concerns: She is worried that a tendon is tearing and that she will have to give up going to the gym and carrying her campus backpack.
expectations: She hopes to get specific stretching exercises and reassurance that nothing is torn.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Rotator cuff tendinopathy evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Rotator cuff tendinopathy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy: Physical therapy (rotator cuff strengthening), NSAIDs, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: aching shoulder pain when reaching overhead

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with aching shoulder pain when reaching overhead. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Rotator cuff tendinopathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rotator cuff tear without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Progressive weakness would suggest tear rather than tendinopathy.
management_principles: Plan for Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy: Physical therapy (rotator cuff strengthening), NSAIDs
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

history.answer: My right shoulder has been aching quite a bit, especially whenever I raise my arm or reach overhead.
It is just the top and outside of my right shoulder. My left shoulder feels completely normal.
It started about three weeks ago and has been gradually getting more noticeable.
It is a dull, deep ache that is around a three out of ten normally, but it flares up to a six when I raise my arm.
Reaching up to high shelves, brushing my hair, and overhead gym workouts or volleyball serves trigger the sharp ache.
Resting my arm down by my side eases the discomfort, while repetitive overhead motions make it much worse.
I do not have real muscle weakness and my arm does not suddenly drop; it is just painful when I try to push through overhead motions.
No, there has been no visible swelling, redness, or warmth over the shoulder.
I do not have morning stiffness, though the shoulder feels a bit stiff if I sleep right on that side.
I can write and use a computer without trouble, but putting on a jacket or reaching behind my back feels uncomfortable.
No, I did not fall or dislocate the shoulder, and I did not hear or feel any popping or snapping sound.
No, I have never had shoulder trouble or joint problems before this.
I have felt generally run down and fatigued lately with college exams, but I have not had fevers or weight loss.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No skin rashes, butterfly rash across my cheeks, mouth ulcers, hair loss, or dry eyes and mouth.
No, I do not have lower back pain in the morning, heel pain, or sausage-like swelling in my fingers or toes.
No recent sore throat, cough, stomach bug, diarrhea, or painful urination.
I eat normal meals without heavy meat binges, and I do not take water pills or diuretic medications.
No, I have never had steroid injections into any joint, joint surgery, or artificial implants.
I have one steady partner, we always use protection, and I have no history of genital discharge or sexually transmitted infections.
I thought I just pulled a muscle from carrying my heavy shoulder bag around campus or maybe slept on it wrong.
I'm worried that something in there is actually tearing and that I won't be able to work out or carry my bag.
I was hoping to get some good stretches to fix it and reassurance that nothing is torn.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter pain relievers, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medicines or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used e-cigarettes.
I only drink socially, about one glass of beer once or twice a month with friends.
I am a college student, and I play recreational volleyball and do gym training twice a week.
No one in my family has rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, gout, or early joint problems.
My last period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every twenty-eight days, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, healthy-appearing young woman sitting comfortably without distress, holding the right upper extremity naturally adducted.

Tenderness over the right subacromial space and greater tuberosity; painful active abduction between 60 and 120 degrees, with preserved passive range of motion and no joint effusion, redness, or heat bilaterally.
Motor strength is 5/5 throughout bilateral upper extremities, with pain provoked during resisted abduction and external rotation on the right but no drop-arm or true weakness.
Full active cervical spine range of motion without midline tenderness or reproduction of arm pain on Spurling maneuver.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation across bilateral upper extremity dermatomes, including the right lateral deltoid area.
Biceps, brachioradialis, and triceps deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally.
Bilateral radial and brachial pulses are 2+ and equal, with brisk capillary refill under two seconds.
No malar rash, psoriatic plaques, tophi, oral ulcerations, or nail changes.
